It needs only its Lord, who has never depended on a Christian culture to do his work, and who is, even now, in the ruins of the old arrangement, building something the church has not seen in a very long time. The study does not resolve. It sends you out to live well in the exile, in hope, without looking back.

keyScripture.why: For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope, spoken to exiles told to settle into their loss, grounding hope not in the restoration of the past but in the God who is bringing a future.

discussion.q: When a familiar world ends, the heart reaches for the past. Where do you feel the pull of nostalgia for a more Christian time, and what exactly are you aching to get back?
discussion.behind: Open by naming the ache honestly and specifically. Nostalgia is powerful and usually unexamined. The aim is to get the particular longing on the table, the Sunday closings, the cultural backing, the ease, so the room can later ask whether that ache is hope or its counterfeit.

discussion.q: Bell says nostalgia is not hope but hope's counterfeit. What is the difference between longing to go back to a Christian past and hoping forward to a kingdom God is bringing?
discussion.behind: Land the central distinction. Nostalgia looks backward to a lost golden age, hope looks forward to a promised future. Help the room feel that these are not the same and that confusing them keeps the church paralyzed, mourning instead of living and working.

discussion.q: Bell grants the past was never as good as we remember, and also that real goods were genuinely lost. How do you hold both, refusing to idolize the past without pretending nothing valuable is gone?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness. The room will tend either to gild the past or to dismiss it. The discipline is to grieve real losses honestly while refusing to make the past an idol. Hold both, and do not let the session collapse into either nostalgia or its smug opposite.

discussion.q: The exiles were not promised the old Jerusalem back unchanged, but a future and a hope they could not yet see. What would it mean for you to hope for something God is bringing that you cannot yet picture?
discussion.behind: Move toward forward-facing hope. We want the specific old thing back, and God offers a future we cannot yet see. Help the room sit with the discomfort and the freedom of hoping for what God is making rather than for what we have lost.

discussion.q: Looking back over all five sessions, what is the one thing you most need to stop carrying, the lost world you keep mourning, and what would it free you to do if you finally set it down?
discussion.behind: Close the whole study with self-implication and release, leader first. Do not resolve it. Invite each person to name what they have been clutching from the old world and what living well in the exile would require. End facing forward, not back. Go first.

objections.objection: The past really was better. Stores closed on Sunday, families were intact, the culture made faith easy, and children grew up knowing right from wrong. The way forward is back, and pretending otherwise is just surrender to decline.
objections.response: Bell grants more of this than the cynic expects. Real goods have been lost, not every change is progress, and a culture that has forgotten the gospel is in measurable ways harsher than one that remembered it dimly. The grief is not foolish and the losses are real. But two things have to be said. First, the remembered golden age is partly a trick of memory. That same Christian culture coexisted with injustices it baptized and crowds of nominal believers it produced, and we tend to remember the order and forget the rot. Second, and more important, even where the past was genuinely better, the way forward is never simply backward, because Christian hope has never once pointed back to a lost golden age. It points forward to a kingdom coming. To make the recovery of the past the object of the church's hope is to put hope in the wrong direction entirely. Grieve the losses. Do not enshrine the past as the thing we are hoping for.

objections.objection: The past was never as good as people remember, so we should stop mourning it and just embrace whatever the future brings. Progress is real, the old world deserved to die, and clinging to it is the whole problem.
objections.response: Grant what is right, because the golden age really is largely a trick of memory, and clinging to a romanticized past is a genuine idolatry that paralyzes the church. But mere acceptance of the future is not hope, and the progressive's confidence has its own blindness. The bland assumption that things will simply work out, that whatever comes next is better because it is next, is not Christian hope and is not even supported by history, which is full of changes that made the world worse. Hope is not optimism about the future in general. It is the confident expectation of a specific future that God himself is bringing, his kingdom, his new creation, his making of all things new. The progressive who merely embraces the future has no more reason for confidence than the nostalgic who clings to the past. Both have detached hope from the only thing that can ground it, which is not the past or the future as such but the God who holds both.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your hope for the church rested entirely on what God is bringing rather than on getting any part of the old world back, what would you stop grieving, and what would you finally be free to start building?
sessions.practice: This week, do one thing that belongs to the future God is bringing rather than to the past you are mourning. Plant something, literally or otherwise, that you may not see come to fruit, an investment in a person, a work, a place, made in hope rather than in defense of what is slipping away. Each time you catch yourself aching for the old world, turn the ache into a prayer for the kingdom that is coming, and write down what changes in you when hope faces forward instead of back.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you did not promise the exiles the old world back. You promised them yourself, present in Babylon, and a future they could not yet see. We confess we have spent our grief facing backward, mourning a Christendom that is gone, when you have been calling us forward the whole time. Heal us of the nostalgia that masquerades as faith. Teach us a hope that does not depend on getting anything back, that rests only on you, who were making all things new long before any of this began and will be making them new long after it is forgotten. Send us out to live well in the exile, to build and plant and bless and love, without looking back, because you are ahead of us, and you are bringing your kingdom. Amen.
reflection: Have I confused nostalgia for a Christian past with Christian hope, and what is the difference between aching to go back and hoping forward to the kingdom God is bringing?
What am I still clutching from the old world that I need to set down in order to live well in the one God has actually placed me in?
If my hope rested entirely on the God who is making all things new and not on any recovery of the past, what would I stop mourning and what would I be free to begin?
sessions.teaching: We have spent four sessions looking hard at the end of Christendom and the church's recovered life as an exilic, creative minority bearing witness without power. And there is one last thing to face, because it is the feeling that can undo all of it, the feeling that hides inside the grief and quietly poisons the hope. Nostalgia. When a familiar world ends, the heart reaches instinctively backward, and the church after Christendom is tempted by a powerful and corrosive longing, the ache to return to a remembered golden age, a time when everything was Christian and ordered and ours, when the stores closed on Sunday and the culture carried us and being a believer cost nothing. So the first question, the one this whole study has been moving toward, is whether that ache is hope at all, or whether it is hope's most convincing counterfeit. Take the two responses at their strongest. The first is the nostalgic's. The past really was better. Families were more intact, the culture made faith easy, children grew up with a shared sense of right and wrong, and the way forward is back, and to say otherwise is just to surrender to decline. And Bell grants more of this than you might expect, because real goods have been lost. Not every change is progress, and a culture that has forgotten the gospel is in measurable ways harsher than one that remembered it even dimly. The grief is not foolish, and the losses are real, and a study that pretended otherwise would be lying to comfort you. The second response is the progressive's. The past was never as good as people remember, so stop mourning it and embrace whatever comes next, because the old world deserved to die and clinging to it is the whole problem. And there is truth here too, because the golden age is largely a trick of memory. That same Christian culture coexisted with injustices it blessed and crowds of merely nominal believers it manufactured, and we are very good at remembering its order and forgetting its rot. Now refuse to let either response win, because this is the hinge of everything. Nostalgia is not hope, which destroys the first response, and the proof is simply this. Christian hope has never once, in the whole of Scripture, pointed backward to a lost golden age. It does not even point back to Eden. The Bible does not end with a return to the garden. It ends with a city coming down, a new creation, a future that is more than the past restored. To make the recovery of Christendom the object of the church's hope is to aim hope in exactly the wrong direction, to spend the energy of the future grieving the past. But mere acceptance of the future is not hope either, which destroys the second response, because the bland confidence that things will work out, that whatever is next is better because it is next, is not Christian hope and is not even true. History is full of changes that made the world worse. Hope is not optimism in general. Hope is the confident expectation of a specific future that God himself is bringing. And this is exactly what the exiles in Babylon were given. Remember the promise from the second session, the one written on the greeting cards, and remember now to whom it was actually written. For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope. That was not spoken to people on their way up. It was spoken to exiles who had lost everything and been told to settle into the loss, to build houses in Babylon and plant gardens in Babylon and wait. And the hope they were given was not the old Jerusalem restored unchanged. It was a future they could not yet see the shape of, grounded entirely in the God who was with them in the exile and who held the future in his hands. So here is where the whole study lands, and it does not land on a strategy. Christian hope runs forward, not backward. It rests not on Christendom restored but on a kingdom coming. It rests on a God who was making all things new long before an emperor named Constantine made the faith respectable, and who will be making them new long after the last great cathedral in the West has become a museum with an admission fee. The church does not actually need its old world back. It never did. It needs only its Lord, the one who has never, not once, depended on a Christian culture to do his work, who built his church under Caesar and Nero with no power and no respectability and no Sundays closed by law, and who is doing the same thing again, right now, in the ruins of the arrangement we are mourning. And I have to end where the honest preacher always has to end, inside the indictment. I have grieved this loss facing the wrong way. I have spent more prayer wanting the old world back than wanting the kingdom to come, and called the nostalgia faithfulness. I have stood at the window like the exiles waiting for a Jerusalem that was not coming, when the word the whole time was, turn around, I am ahead of you, build here, I am bringing something you cannot yet see. So I will not tie this study off with a tidy ending, because the exile does not have a tidy ending and pretending it does would betray everything we have said. I will end it the way Jeremiah ended his letter, by sending you out to live. Build your houses. Plant your gardens. Seek the welfare of the city. Be a creative minority, distinct and good and unafraid of being small. Bear your witness without power, by a love no one can explain. And do all of it in hope, the real kind, the kind that faces forward, because the God who is gentle and faithful and ahead of us is not finished, and the best thing the church can do with the end of Christendom is to stop looking back at what is gone and start living toward what is coming. He is bringing his kingdom. Live like it. And do not look back.

scriptureStudy.note: I know the plans I have for you, to give you a future and a hope. Spoken to exiles told to settle into their loss, the verse grounds hope not in a restored past but in the God who holds and is bringing the future.

Remember not the former things, behold I am doing a new thing. God explicitly tells his people to stop facing backward, because his work is ahead of them, a new thing springing forth that nostalgia would cause them to miss.

Forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal. Paul models a hope that refuses to live in the past, even a glorious one, and runs toward the future God is bringing.

They acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth, desiring a better country, a heavenly one. The faithful did not long to return to the land they had left but hoped forward to a city God was preparing.
Behold, I am making all things new. The Bible ends not with a return to a lost garden but with a new creation and a city coming down, the forward shape of all Christian hope.
No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God. Jesus names the backward look as a disqualification for kingdom work, a sharp word against nostalgia that paralyzes.

In this hope we were saved, but hope that is seen is not hope, for we wait for it with patience. Hope is by definition for what is not yet visible, which is why it can never be the recovery of a remembered past.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the difference between hope and optimism, and the deeper question of what kind of age we actually live in, because the whole study has assumed a diagnosis that deserves to be named directly. The philosopher Charles Taylor, in his account of what he calls a secular age, argues that the deepest change in the modern West is not that fewer people believe but that the conditions of belief have shifted, so that faith, once the unquestioned default, has become one contested option among many, surrounded by what he calls cross-pressures that make every position feel fragile. This is the real water the church now swims in, and it explains why the loss is not merely a loss of numbers but a loss of plausibility, the sense that the gospel is simply assumed. Set Taylor's diagnosis beside Augustine, who wrote The City of God as another familiar Christian-seeming world, the Roman order, was collapsing, and who refused both the pagan nostalgia that blamed the Christians for Rome's fall and the Christian triumphalism that confused the empire with the kingdom. Augustine taught the church to see two cities intermingled throughout history, the city of man and the city of God, and to set its hope not on any earthly city, however Christian it looked, but on the city of God that does not pass away. A serious group should hold Taylor and Augustine together. Taylor names the present condition with precision, and Augustine, sixteen centuries earlier and at the end of his own Christendom, names the hope that survives it. The discipline is to grasp that the church has stood at the end of a world before, watched a Christian-seeming order fall, and learned then what it must learn again now, that its hope was never in the order that was passing but in the God whose city is still coming, and that this is precisely why the church can let the old world go without despair and live well in the new one without illusion.
sessions.caseStudy: An older believer, faithful his whole life, found himself sinking into a quiet despair as he watched the church and the culture he had known come apart. He kept telling his grandson that everything had been better before, that the real Christianity was behind them, that there was nothing left to do but hold on and mourn. The grandson, who loved Jesus but had never known the world the old man missed, finally said something that landed hard. Grandpa, he said, you keep talking about the church like it already died, but the church I am part of is alive, just different, and it scares you because it does not look like yours. The old man went home unsettled, and over weeks he began to notice that his grief was always facing backward, that he prayed more for the return of the past than for the coming of the kingdom, and that somewhere along the way he had quietly started hoping in Christendom instead of in Christ. He did not get the old world back, and he stopped asking for it. What he found instead was that when his hope turned forward, toward the God who was making all things new, the despair lifted, not because the losses were not real but because they were no longer the last word. He spent his final years investing in the young people of that strange new church, planting things he would not live to see grow. Use his story to help the group tell nostalgia from hope, to see how grief facing backward becomes despair and grief facing forward becomes freedom, and to name what each of them is being invited to plant in hope rather than to mourn in defeat.

memoryVerse.text: For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope.

leaderPrimer: Someone in your group wants their country back. He may say it in those words, as a man once said to the writer of this study after a service, or he may simply carry it, the ache for stores closed on Sunday, prayer before kickoff, a world where the culture did half the church's work for it. Nostalgia is the hazard of this room, and it is subtle because it wears the clothes of faithfulness. A leader is tempted to handle it in one of two cheap ways. Join the funeral and spend five weeks mourning together, which feels pastoral and forms nobody. Or sneer at it, playing the enlightened guide correcting sentimental people, which loses the room in one evening and deserves to. Refuse both. The grief in front of you is real, some of what died deserved mourning, and the study's whole argument is that Christendom was an arrangement and not the faith, so a leader has to hold the loss and the hope in the same hand without dropping either. The writer holds them from inside a small Michigan pastorate, where the end of the arrangement is not a thesis but the view from the pulpit, and he still argues that the church has been here before and done some of its best work here. Watch for two people especially. The angry one, for whom every session sounds like surrender, needs to hear that exile is not defeat, that Jeremiah told the exiles to build houses and plant gardens in Babylon precisely because God was not finished with them (Jeremiah 29). And the relieved one, often younger, glad to watch cultural Christianity die, needs the harder word that contempt is not a posture either, and that nobody builds a creative minority out of scorn for their grandparents. Sessions four and five carry the constructive weight of the study, so do not let the group spend itself on lament before it arrives there. The aim is a room that stops asking how to get the old world back and starts asking what faithfulness looks like in the world that actually exists. Lead like a settler, not a mourner. Plant something.

faq.q: Is this study just telling Christians to give up and accept cultural defeat?
faq.a: No, and it works hard to prevent exactly that reading. The end of Christendom is not the defeat of the church, and the study insists on the difference. What is ending is a cultural arrangement, the centuries-old situation in which the surrounding society did much of the church's work for it and made belief easy and respectable. That arrangement is passing, and the study grants real goods are passing with it. But the church itself is not ending, and the study points repeatedly to the early church, which had no cultural power at all and turned the Roman world upside down. The call is not to surrender but to recover the church's oldest and most fruitful condition, an exilic, creative minority that bears witness by a way of life rather than by the levers of power. That is not defeat. It is, the study argues, the church being handed back its native vocation.

faq.q: Are you saying Christendom was a bad thing?
faq.a: Partly, and refusing to flatten that is the point. Christendom did real good across many centuries, building hospitals and universities and slowly bending a brutal world toward the memory of a crucified God, and the study grieves the genuine goods that are passing with it. But Christendom was also a compromise. The marriage of the faith with political power produced inquisitions and state churches that persecuted dissenters, and it filled the pews with crowds of people who were baptized into a culture and never converted to a Lord. The study refuses both the nostalgia that remembers only the order and the contempt that remembers only the rot. Christendom was an arrangement with a beginning you can date to the fourth century and an end we are now living through, and the honest posture toward its passing is grief and relief at once, never a simple verdict in either direction.

faq.q: If the culture is hostile, should not we fight to take it back?
faq.a: The study takes that instinct seriously and then redirects it. Christians may not retreat into a private faith and abandon public life, and engagement in the common good is legitimate and even commanded. But the study argues that power is not the engine of witness, and the proof is the early church, which had no courts, no schools, no laws, and no votes, and converted an empire anyway, from the bottom up, by a way of life so visibly different that the watching world could not look away. When the church pours its hope into seizing cultural and political power, it tends to get the power and lose the witness, becoming just another faction grabbing for advantage. The study calls instead for witness without power, a costly, visible love that cannot coerce and so can only attract, which is the only kind of witness that ever changed anyone from the inside.

faq.q: What does it mean to live as exiles, and is not that a depressing way to see the church?
faq.a: It is the opposite of depressing once you see where the image comes from. When the people of Judah were carried to Babylon, Jeremiah sent them a letter telling them not to revolt and not to assimilate, but to build houses, plant gardens, and seek the welfare of the very city that had conquered them, because God was present with them there. Exile in this sense is not exile from God but a way of being faithfully present in a culture you do not control, neither fighting it nor dissolving into it. And it is the church's oldest self-understanding. Peter calls his readers exiles. The early Christians described themselves as living in every country as sojourners. Christendom made the church forget it was an exilic people and imagine itself as the establishment. The end of Christendom simply returns the church to the condition in which it has usually done its best work, present, distinct, and seeking the good of the place where God has sent it.

faq.q: What is a creative minority, and how is it different from a holy huddle?
faq.a: A creative minority is a small people who accept that they are small, refuse both bitterness and dissolution, and turn their distinctiveness into a gift to the wider world rather than a wall against it. The difference from a holy huddle is everything. A holy huddle is distinct against the world, hoarding its purity, withdrawing, looking down on outsiders. A creative minority is distinct for the sake of the world, contributing to the common good precisely out of the depth of its difference. The early church was a creative minority before the phrase existed. Its strange disciplines, refusing infanticide, caring for the poor and the enemy and the dead, a different way with money and the body, were not a fortress but a gift, and much of what the West later called humane grew from them. The test of true distinctiveness is whether it makes the church a gift or a fortress, and the study presses relentlessly toward the gift.

faq.q: Is the church doomed because it is shrinking?
faq.a: No, and the study challenges the assumption underneath the question, that influence requires numbers. History disproves it repeatedly. The most influential minority in human history is arguably the Jewish people, who shaped the law, ethics, and moral imagination of whole civilizations while remaining a tiny fraction of the population, precisely by being distinct rather than many. The early church was a fraction of a percent of the Roman Empire and reshaped it from below. A creative minority works not by outvoting the culture but by out-living it. So a smaller church is not automatically a defeated one. It may be a freer and more potent one, released from the temptations of power and respectability and returned to the methods that actually changed the ancient world, patience, costly love, and the slow formation of a distinct people. Smallness is not the same as irrelevance.

faq.q: Is not longing for a more Christian past a good and faithful thing?
faq.a: The study draws a careful line here, because the longing is understandable but can be a trap. It grants that real goods have been lost and that not every change is progress, so the grief is not foolish. But it insists that nostalgia is not the same as hope, and is in fact hope's counterfeit. Christian hope has never once pointed backward to a lost golden age. The Bible does not even end with a return to Eden. It ends with a city coming down and a new creation, a future that is more than the past restored. To make the recovery of Christendom the object of the church's hope is to aim hope in exactly the wrong direction, spending the energy of the future mourning the past. The study calls for grief that faces forward, hope grounded not in getting the old world back but in the God who is bringing his kingdom, who was making all things new long before Constantine and will be long after the last cathedral is a museum.

faq.q: How is Christian hope different from just being optimistic that things will work out?
faq.a: Sharply different, and the study is careful to say so. Optimism is the bland assumption that the future will be fine because it is the future, that whatever comes next is better because it is next, and that confidence is not even supported by history, which is full of changes that made the world worse. Christian hope is not optimism in general. It is the confident expectation of a specific future that God himself is bringing, his kingdom, his new creation, his making of all things new. The exiles in Babylon were given a future and a hope, but it was not a vague sense that things would improve. It was grounded entirely in the faithfulness of the God who held the future. The study warns that the progressive who merely embraces the future has no more reason for confidence than the nostalgic who clings to the past. Both have cut hope loose from the only thing that can ground it, which is the God who holds past and future alike.

faq.q: Who are the thinkers behind this study, and do I need to know them to lead it?
faq.a: You do not need to know them to lead it, but they stand behind it and a curious group may want to meet them. Charles Taylor names the present as a secular age, in which belief has shifted from the unquestioned default to one contested option among many, which explains why the church faces a loss of plausibility and not merely of numbers. Lesslie Newbigin argued that the only real defense of the gospel in such an age is a community that actually lives it, the congregation as the lens through which the world reads the good news. Stanley Hauerwas insists the church's first task is not to make the nation just but simply to be the church. Alan Kreider recovered the patience of the early church and how it grew without power. And Augustine, writing The City of God as the Roman order fell, taught the church to set its hope not on any earthly city but on the city of God that does not pass away. The study paraphrases and points to them, but the readings carry everything you need.

faq.q: Does the study expect the church to win the culture back by the end?
faq.a: No, and it deliberately refuses to promise that, because winning the culture back is the wrong goal. The study ends without resolution, on purpose, because the exile does not resolve on a schedule and a study that promised a tidy recovery would be lying. The point is not the restoration of Christendom but the faithful presence of the church in its absence, a creative minority living well in exile, bearing witness without power, hoping forward toward the kingdom God is bringing. For some that will mean grieving real losses honestly. For some it will mean laying down a culture-war reflex. For all of it the promise is not a strategy that succeeds but a Lord who is faithful, who has never depended on a Christian culture to do his work, and who is building something even now in the ruins of the old arrangement. What the study offers is not a victory you achieve but a way of living you receive, present, distinct, and unafraid.

faq.q: Why does the study keep implicating the writer and the leader instead of just diagnosing the culture?
faq.a: Because that is the method, and the method is the honesty. Bell does not stand outside the loss as a prophet announcing other people's failures. He pastored through the years the pews thinned. He watched his assumptions about a Christian America fall apart. He admits he built more of his ministry on cultural Christianity than on Christ, counted respectable crowds as fruit, reached for power because being a small distinct church felt like defeat, and prayed more for the old world to return than for the kingdom to come. He writes from inside the loss and the nostalgia, and the study asks every leader to do the same, because you cannot lead a room through a grief you have not felt or out of a nostalgia you are secretly nursing. A leader who can say I have been mourning the wrong way too can lead without contempt and without distance. A study that pointed only at the culture's failures would let everyone off the hook and change no one.

faq.q: I am a skeptic, and the church losing its grip seems like progress to me. Why should I engage this?
faq.a: It is a fair position, and the study tries to earn the right to answer it by agreeing with more of it than you might expect. It grants that Christendom was deeply compromised, that the marriage of faith and power did real harm, and that crowds of merely cultural Christians were a spiritual problem and not a glory. It does not ask you to mourn the passing of the church's power, and it is suspicious of that power itself. What it offers instead is a claim worth weighing, that the church was at its most humane and most compelling precisely when it had no power at all, when it stayed in the plague cities to nurse the dying, rescued the infants its world threw away, and loved the enemies everyone else hated. Much of what you likely value, the dignity of the weak and the stranger, grew from exactly those strange disciplines. You can weigh whether a powerless, serving church is a thing worth having around. The study does not ask you to pretend.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I am genuinely afraid for the future of the church?
faq.a: Your fear is not a disqualification, and you do not have to hide it. The study is built to be led by a fellow exile, not by someone who has conquered all anxiety about the future and now dispenses calm, and every discussion question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than strategy, so you are not improvising. Your honesty about your own fear may be the most pastoral thing in the room, the permission that lets others stop pretending they are fine. What you do need is to refuse to turn the study into either a rally or a wake, to hold the room in honest grief and honest hope at once, and to keep pointing everyone, yourself first, toward the God who is ahead of us, who has never needed a Christian culture to do his work, and who is building something now in the ruins of the old one. Read the leader primer, settle your own heart, find where your own hope has been facing backward, and trust the material to carry the rest.

timeline.event: Jerusalem falls and Judah is carried into exile in Babylon, and the prophet Jeremiah sends a letter telling the captives not to revolt and not to assimilate but to build houses, plant gardens, and seek the welfare of the city, establishing the charter for a people called to live faithfully in a culture they do not control.

Daniel, an exile who served the Babylonian and Persian courts with excellence while refusing to bow to their gods or stop praying to his own, models the resident alien who is fully present and fully distinct, neither in revolt nor in surrender.

Jesus tells Pilate his kingdom is not of this world, and teaches that his people are salt and light and a city on a hill, locating the church's power in distinct visible goodness rather than in the seizure of worldly rule.

Peter writes to scattered Christians across the empire, addressing them as elect exiles and sojourners and urging an honorable life among the nations, framing the church from the start as a dispersed minority rather than an establishment.

Great plagues sweep the Roman cities, and while many who can afford to flee, Christians stay to nurse the sick and dying, including strangers and enemies, and the church's reputation and numbers rise as a result, a witness of costly love without any power behind it.

The Edict of Milan, issued under Constantine, makes Christianity legal across the empire, beginning the long shift the historians call the Constantinian settlement, in which the church gains power and respectability and slowly trades the conditions that made it strange and compelling.

Rome is sacked by the Goths, and Augustine writes The City of God, refusing both the pagan nostalgia that blames the Christians and the triumphalism that confuses the empire with the kingdom, teaching the church to set its hope on the city of God that does not pass away rather than on any earthly order.

Benedict establishes his monastic rule, and across the centuries that follow small disciplined communities preserve learning, prayer, and agriculture through the collapse of the old order, a creative minority that ends up reseeding a civilization without ever seizing power.

The Enlightenment reshapes the intellectual world of the West, and over the following centuries belief begins to shift from the unquestioned background of life toward one contested option among many, the slow erosion of the conditions that made Christendom feel natural.

Lesslie Newbigin, returning from decades as a missionary in India, begins to see the West itself as a mission field, and later argues that the only real defense of the gospel in a post-Christian culture is a congregation that lives it, the church as the hermeneutic of the gospel.

Stanley Hauerwas and others press the conviction that the church's first political task is not to make the nation just but simply to be the church, a distinct community whose common life is itself a witness, sharpening the call for the church to stop reaching for the levers of power.

Charles Taylor publishes A Secular Age, arguing that the deepest modern change is not that fewer people believe but that the conditions of belief have shifted, so that faith has become fragile and contested rather than assumed, naming with precision the water the church now swims in.

Alan Kreider publishes The Patient Ferment of the Early Church, recovering how the powerless early church grew not through programs or pressure but through patience and the slow formation of a way of life so distinct that a watching world was drawn in over time.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here, and thank you for the willingness it takes, because the world we are going to talk about, the one that is ending, is one many of us have feelings about that are hard to say out loud. Before we start, three things. First, this is an honest room. You can grieve the passing of a Christian culture here without being called faithless, and you can feel relief at its passing here without being called disloyal. Both are welcome, because both are partly right. Second, this study refuses two easy roads. It will not turn into a rally to take the culture back, and it will not turn into a wake for a church that is finished. The whole point is a third way, the patient and hopeful life of an exilic people who build and plant and bless the place God has sent them. Third, the writer puts himself inside all of this, and so will I. I have grieved the wrong way. I have leaned on a Christian culture more than on Christ. We are not diagnosing other people's failures from a safe distance. We are the exiles. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what the passage says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the actual world we live in, into the workplace and the neighborhood and the family table where the culture has changed under our feet, because that is where this either matters or it does not.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not resolved, because the exile does not resolve on a schedule and pretending otherwise would be a lie. Take the weight of this toward the kingdom that is coming this week, rather than carrying it backward toward the world that is gone. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if something in tonight has you facing backward, grieving the past more than you are hoping for the kingdom, hear that gently as an invitation to turn around, because God is ahead of us. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for the honesty it took to be in this room.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules that grief and relief are both welcome and the study will be neither a rally nor a wake, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly. Name plainly the difference between Christianity and Christendom.
Week 2: Session 1, The End of Christendom, full discussion and practice, with extended time on what was genuinely good and what was genuinely compromised.
Week 3: Session 2, A Letter to the Exiles, part one through Jeremiah's letter and the refusal of both revolt and surrender.
Week 4: Session 2 continued, Daniel as the model of present-and-distinct, plus the practice of seeking the welfare of an actual place.
Week 5: Session 3, Witness Without Power, the early church's costly love and Newbigin's congregation as the lens for the gospel.
Week 6: Session 4, A Creative Minority, the third way between the defensive and the assimilated minority and the disciplines that bless.
Week 7: Session 5, Hope Without Nostalgia, the difference between nostalgia and hope and the forward shape of Christian expectation.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and what each person is being freed to set down and to build, with space for the room to face forward together.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the end of Christendom and the letter to the exiles.
Week 2: Session 3, Witness Without Power, with extended time on the early church's costly love and the difference between attracting and compelling.
Week 3: Session 4, A Creative Minority, the third way and the disciplines that make the church oddly good.
Week 4: Session 5, Hope Without Nostalgia, plus a short integration close facing forward toward the kingdom God is bringing.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, The End of Christendom.
Week 2: Session 2, A Letter to the Exiles.

bibliography.title: A Secular Age
bibliography.author: Charles Taylor
bibliography.note: The major account of how belief in the West shifted from the unquestioned default to one contested option among many, naming the conditions the church now lives in. Background for the whole study and especially session 5. Leader to confirm specific claims before pressing them as settled.

bibliography.title: The Gospel in a Pluralist Society
bibliography.author: Lesslie Newbigin
bibliography.note: The argument that the only real defense of the gospel in a post-Christian culture is a community that lives it, the congregation as the hermeneutic of the gospel. The pastoral spine of session 3.

bibliography.title: Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony
bibliography.author: Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon
bibliography.note: The case that the church is a distinct colony of resident aliens whose first task is to be the church rather than to manage the nation. Anchors sessions 2 and 4.

bibliography.title: The Patient Ferment of the Early Church
bibliography.author: Alan Kreider
bibliography.note: On how the powerless early church grew through patience and the slow formation of a distinct way of life rather than through programs or pressure. Background for sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: The City of God
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Written as the Roman order collapsed, refusing both pagan nostalgia and Christian triumphalism, teaching the church to hope in the city of God and not in any earthly order. Background for sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Rise of Christianity
bibliography.author: Rodney Stark
bibliography.note: A sociologist's account of how the early church grew, including its costly care during the plagues and its refusal of the casual cruelty of its age. Supports sessions 3 and 4. Leader to confirm specifics before attributing them to Bell.

bibliography.title: The Letter to Diognetus
bibliography.author: Anonymous, early Christian
bibliography.note: An early text describing Christians as living in every country as sojourners, sharing everything as citizens and enduring everything as foreigners. Background for the exile theme in session 2.

bibliography.title: Jeremiah and the wider Old Testament exile narratives
bibliography.author: Various, Scripture
bibliography.note: Jeremiah's letter to the exiles and the Daniel and Esther and Nehemiah accounts of faithful life under foreign power. The biblical foundation for sessions 2 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Dignity of Difference and writings on the creative minority
bibliography.author: Jonathan Sacks
bibliography.note: On the vocation of a people to be a creative minority, distinct enough to preserve a way of life and generous enough to bless the world. Anchors session 4. Leader to confirm specifics before stating them as the study's position.

bibliography.title: After Virtue
bibliography.author: Alasdair MacIntyre
bibliography.note: The diagnosis of a fragmented moral culture that ends by calling for new forms of community to sustain virtue through a dark age, a touchstone for the creative-minority idea. Offered as a balancing voice for session 4. Leader to confirm before pressing the argument as the study's own.

bibliography.title: The Benedict Option
bibliography.author: Rod Dreher
bibliography.note: A widely discussed proposal for distinct Christian community in a post-Christian age, useful as a conversation partner that the study engages critically rather than endorses, since it must be tested against the call to bless and not only to withdraw. Leader to confirm and weigh before attributing claims.

bibliography.title: To Change the World
bibliography.author: James Davison Hunter
bibliography.note: On the limits of the church's strategies for cultural power and the alternative of faithful presence, paralleling the study's witness-without-power argument. Supports session 3. Leader to confirm specifics before pressing them as Bell's own.

furtherReading: The Patient Ferment of the Early Church, Alan Kreider, for readers who want to sit longer with how a powerless church grew through patience and a distinct way of life.
The Gospel in a Pluralist Society, Lesslie Newbigin, for those who want the fuller argument that the church's life is the lens through which the world reads the gospel, which anchors session 3.

Resident Aliens, Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon, for anyone wrestling with what it means for the church to be a distinct colony rather than the establishment, leader to confirm specific claims.
A Secular Age, Charles Taylor, an enormous book best read in summary first, for readers who want to understand why belief itself feels different now and not merely less common.
The City of God, Augustine, for those who want to see the church at the end of an earlier Christian-seeming world learning the hope that survives such an ending.

glossary.definition: The long cultural arrangement, beginning roughly in the fourth century and now ending, in which the Christian faith was the established religion of a society and the surrounding culture did much of the church's work for it, making belief easy, respectable, and often merely nominal.

Belief that is carried more by the surrounding society than by personal conversion, the Christianity of a person who is Christian because everyone around them is, which Christendom produced in large numbers and whose passing the study treats as a clarifying mercy.

The biblical condition, modeled by Judah in Babylon and named by Peter for the church, of living faithfully as a distinct people within a culture one does not control, neither in revolt against it nor assimilated into it, seeking its welfare while belonging to God.

Peter's image of the church as sojourners and exiles, fully present in a society as good neighbors and yet not finally belonging to it, with a citizenship that is in heaven, the church's recovered self-understanding after Christendom.

A small people who accept that they are small, refuse both bitterness and dissolution, and turn their distinctiveness into a gift to the wider world, contributing to the common good out of the depth of their difference rather than in spite of it.

Bearing witness to the gospel not by seizing or defending cultural and political power but by a costly, visible way of life that cannot coerce and so can only attract, the method by which the powerless early church converted an empire.

The shift that began when the emperor Constantine made Christianity legal and then favored, after which the church gained power and respectability and gradually lost the conditions that had made it a strange and compelling minority.
The ache to return to a remembered golden age, treated by the study as hope's counterfeit, because Christian hope has never pointed backward to a lost past but forward to the kingdom God is bringing.

Not optimism that things will work out in general, but the confident expectation of a specific future that God himself is bringing, his kingdom and his new creation, grounded in the faithfulness of God rather than in the past or the future as such.

Charles Taylor's name for the present condition of the West, in which belief has shifted from the unquestioned background of life to one contested and fragile option among many, so that the loss the church faces is one of plausibility and not merely of numbers.

Newbigin's phrase for the local congregation as the lens through which a watching world reads what the gospel actually means, making the visible life of the church its primary witness in a culture that no longer assumes the message.

Augustine's framework from The City of God, the city of man and the city of God intermingled throughout history, teaching the church to set its hope not on any earthly order, however Christian it appears, but on the city of God that does not pass away.

The posture of being fully and distinctly present in a culture for its good, neither withdrawing from it nor seizing power over it, the practical shape of seeking the welfare of the city while remaining the people of God.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: The Christian culture many of us grew up with is ending, and the church keeps reaching for one of two useless responses, panic that fights to take it all back or despair that gives up. There is a third way. This five-session study, drawn from James Bell's After Christendom, walks slowly through what has actually ended and why it may be a mercy, the church learning to live as exiles the way Jeremiah told the captives in Babylon to live, witness offered without power, becoming a creative minority rather than a defeated one, and a hope that does not run on nostalgia. It is honest about what is lost and clear about what is coming. Built so any volunteer can lead it with no prep. Come honest, not finished.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We are starting a five-week study on following Jesus faithfully in a world that no longer pretends to be Christian, drawn from After Christendom, and before anyone braces, hear this. It is not a rally to win the culture back, and it is not a wake for a church that is finished. It takes the loss seriously, names what was genuinely good and what was genuinely compromised, and points us toward the church's oldest and most fruitful condition, an exilic, creative minority that turned the ancient world upside down with no power at all. It implicates the preacher first, because I have grieved the wrong way too. No homework, and no prep needed to lead a group. If the changing world has unsettled you, this is for you. Sign up at the welcome table.

quoteCards: What is ending is not the church. It is the scaffolding. Christendom was never the gospel.
Jeremiah told the exiles to build houses and plant gardens in Babylon, because God was present in the exile and not only back in Jerusalem.
Power can compel, but it cannot convert. A faith that attracts when it could not coerce is the only kind that ever changed anyone from the inside.
Smallness is not the same as irrelevance. A church that is small and distinct and good can shape a culture a large and bland one never could.
The early church rescued the infants its world threw away. Its difference was not a wall it built but a gift it gave.
Nostalgia is not hope. It is hope's counterfeit. Christian hope has never once pointed backward to a lost golden age.
The Bible does not end with a return to the garden. It ends with a city coming down, and all things made new.
The church does not need its old world back. It needs only its Lord, who has never depended on a Christian culture to do his work.
